questions.prompt: A Kotlin cache stores two values in a set: `data class Entry(val key: String) { var hits: Int = 0 }`. Both entries have key `home`, but their body properties `hits` are 1 and 9. No generated functions are overridden. What is the set size after adding both?

choices.text: 2: every declared property participates in equality.
1: generated equality compares the primary-constructor key, excluding hits.
2: data classes use object identity when inserted into a set.
It cannot compile because data classes cannot have body properties.

questions.explanation: Only key participates in generated equality and hashing. Equal keys therefore identify one set element; different hits values do not distinguish them. Body properties are permitted but excluded from these generated functions.

sources.title: Data classes | Kotlin Documentation
sources.claim: Generated equality and hashing use primary-constructor properties; body properties are excluded.

questions.prompt:
```kotlin
open class Screen
class Detail : Screen()
fun Screen.label() = "base"
fun Detail.label() = "detail"
val widened: Screen = Detail()
val concrete = Detail()
```
Neither class has a label member. What pair do `widened.label()` and `concrete.label()` produce?

choices.text: detail, detail: both objects have the runtime type Detail.
base, base: extensions always use the root receiver.
base, detail: each call uses its expression's declared or inferred receiver type.
The calls are ambiguous because both extension names are the same.

questions.explanation: The widened expression has static type Screen, while concrete has inferred type Detail. Extension resolution uses that compile-time receiver type, so the calls select different extensions despite both objects being Detail instances.

sources.title: Extensions | Kotlin Documentation
sources.claim: Extension function resolution uses the compile-time receiver type rather than the runtime object type.
